text:
Your prompt asks for a painkiller; the crash is a symptom. Rewrite it to ask for the disease and the cure.

**What to ask instead:**

> Investigate this crash and its root cause, not just the symptom:
> `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading "webContents")` at main.js:212 when a window is closed during an update download.
>
> 1. Explain *why* it happens — which object is undefined, when it's torn down, and what lifecycle ordering produces the race (window close vs. update-download callback/event).
> 2. Fix it at the root: guard against stale/destroyed windows, and audit every place in the update flow that touches `window`, `webContents`, or `BrowserWindow` for the same class of bug.
> 3. Make the failure impossible, not just caught: e.g., track window lifetime explicitly, cancel/ignore in-flight update events on teardown, and centralize "is this window still valid?" logic.
> 4. Add a regression test (or a repeatable repro) that closes a window mid-download and asserts no crash.
> 5. Report any other latent races you find in this area, even if I didn't ask.

**Why this is better:**
- **Root cause over patch** — a try/catch at line 212 hides the race and it resurfaces elsewhere.
- **Class-of-bug audit** — one undefined `webContents` almost always means several. Ask for all of them.
- **Prevention** — ask for the invariant (window lifetime) to be enforced, not just this call site.
- **Verification** — demand a repro/test, so "fixed" is provable.
- **Scope expansion** — invite the model to surface nearby issues instead of stopping at the first green.

The general move: ask "why, everywhere, permanently, proven" instead of "make this error go away."

Instead of a point fix, ask for the class of bug to be solved. Rewrite the request around the underlying design flaw:

**Ambitious version:**

> Our Electron app crashes with `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading "webContents")` (main.js:212) when a user closes a window mid-update-download. I don't want a one-line null check — I want the root cause eliminated.
>
> Audit the window and background-service *lifecycle* in the main process: every place we hold a `BrowserWindow` reference, every async callback, and every event handler that fires after `closed`/`destroyed`. The bug is a race between window teardown and an in-flight update. Find all instances of this pattern, not just line 212.
>
> Then propose a fix at the right layer — e.g. a safe accessor/guard, a lifecycle token that async work checks before touching a window, or moving update logic off the per-window object entirely — and tell me the tradeoffs. Add a test that reproduces the race, and show me how to detect these crashes in production (crash reporting, structured logs) so we catch the next variant before users do.

What this buys you: it fixes the whole *category* (destroyed/undefined references during async work), prevents recurrence, and leaves you with observability — for roughly the same effort as the narrow ask.

The one thing I'd verify before sending: whether the update logic *needs* a window reference at all. If not, the most ambitious fix is architectural — decouple updates from UI lifetime so the race can't exist.

Your original ask treats a symptom. The crash is one instance of a whole class: an async update-download callback holding a window reference (or `getAllWindows()[0]`) that gets destroyed mid-flight, then dereferencing `.webContents`. Fixing line 212 with a null check hides it until the next dangling reference bites. Ask for the class, not the instance.

A more ambitious version asks the model to:

**1. Find the root cause, not the line.** Explain *why* the reference is dead (window closed during download), map every async path in the update flow, and identify all places that touch a window across an `await`/callback boundary — not just line 212.

**2. Fix the whole class.** Have it audit `main.js` (and the update module) for every dangling-window access: `BrowserWindow.getAllWindows()[0]`, cached `win`/`win.webContents` in event handlers, listeners not removed on `closed`. Propose one durable pattern (guard helper, `win.isDestroyed()` checks, or holding state off the window) and apply it consistently.

**3. Redesign the update flow if needed.** Should the updater depend on a window at all? Decouple update progress/state from window lifetime so closing a window is a non-event. Ask it to sketch the correct lifecycle before coding.

**4. Add regression coverage.** A test that closes a window mid-download and asserts no crash, so this can't silently return.

**5. Add diagnostics.** Better error capture/telemetry on the update path so the next lifecycle bug is visible instead of blank.

A concrete replacement prompt:

> Our Electron app crashes with `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading "webContents")` in main.js:212 when a user closes a window during an update download. Treat this as a symptom of a class of bug: dangling `BrowserWindow`/`webContents` references accessed across async boundaries. First, root-cause it and map every place in the update flow and window lifecycle where a destroyed window could be dereferenced. Then propose the correct lifecycle design (ideally decoupling the updater from window lifetime), implement a single durable fix applied everywhere, add a regression test that closes a window mid-download, and improve crash diagnostics on that path. Show me the design before you write code.

Two things that make the reframe pay off: **"show the design before code"** prevents a rushed patch, and **"one durable pattern applied everywhere"** stops this from recurring in a different file next week.

## Ambition ladder — Electron `webContents` crash

**Rung 0 (baseline).** Fix the `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading "webContents")` at `main.js:212` when a window is closed during an update download.

---

**Rung 1 — Altitude: fix the lifecycle, not the line.**

> "Make our Electron app crash-free across all window-teardown and update interactions. Build the durable workflow that keeps it that way: group crash reports by signature, add a deterministic reproduction harness for close-vs-update races, and gate releases on a regression test in CI. Report the crash-free-session rate before/after."

- **Judge:** crash-free-session rate from telemetry + a CI test that fails on the old build.
- **Access:** the repo, your crash telemetry (Sentry/Crashpad), CI you can edit.
- **Costs:** you change a workflow — every teardown bug now must come with a repro, and releases wait on it. Time: hours, not minutes.

**Rung 2 — Depth: assume line 212 is one instance of a class.**

> "Treat this crash as a symptom. Model main-process `BrowserWindow` lifecycle as a state machine, then audit *every* `webContents` access reachable from `close`, `closed`, `destroyed`, and update-download events. Deliver: (a) a minimal deterministic repro that fails before the fix and passes after; (b) a fix that removes the whole class, not a lone null guard; (c) a lifecycle fuzzer test that spawns real windows and races close against update events. Unreasonable target: zero use-after-destroy accesses app-wide."

- **Judge:** the fails-then-passes repro; an audit table of all `webContents` access sites; the fuzzer returning zero failures.
- **Access:** full source, ability to run Electron and its test harness locally.
- **Costs:** needs a runnable Electron/CI environment; touches more code than you'd expect; some risk of scope creep.

**Rung 3 — Range: put a crew on it.**

Run these as parallel subagents:
1. **Concurrency specialist** — builds the deterministic interleaving; artefact: race trace.
2. **Electron API expert** — knows `isDestroyed()`/`webContents` semantics; artefact: hardened code.
3. **SRE/observability** — artifacts: crash signature grouping + dashboard.
4. **Test engineer** — artefact: lifecycle fuzzer.
5. **Adversary (required)** — job is to *still* crash it via another teardown path; artefact: a successful attack or a signed-off "can't".

- **Judge:** the adversary either breaks it (iterate) or fails to; fuzzer stays green.
- **Access:** granted ability to install deps, run the app under a headless/CI Electron, and read telemetry.
- **Costs:** highest prerequisite bar; needs compute and CI permissions.

**Rung 4 — Combined.** All of the above: altitudinal target (crash-free session rate sustained by telemetry + CI), depth target (whole class eliminated, deterministic repro, fuzzer), range target (five-discipline crew with an adversary). Judge = telemetry trend + adversarial failure. Access = repo, telemetry, CI, install permissions.

**Axes that don't apply:** none — all three apply cleanly here.

---

**Recommendation: Rung 2.** It's the highest rung whose prerequisites you almost certainly have today (the repo + a runnable Electron environment), and it turns a one-line patch into a reproduced, verified fix of the *entire* race class. Step up to Rung 3 the moment you can grant CI edits and crash-telemetry access — that's when the workflow becomes self-sustaining.

## Baseline (rung 0)
Fix the `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading "webContents")` crash at main.js:212, which fires when a window is closed mid-update. Domain: Electron main-process lifecycle. Role: app developer. Materials: the stack trace, main.js, an updater.

---

**Axis check up front**
- **Altitude** — applies. "Fix this crash" recurs as a class ("keep the app from crashing during updates").
- **Depth** — applies. The professional rewrite changes the method, not just the vocabulary.
- **Range** — applies. Reliability, test, and adversarial disciplines each add an artefact.
- **Speed** — explicitly out of scope per the skill.

---

## Rung 1 — Altitude: aim at the outcome, not the line

**Prompt to paste:**
> Our Electron app throws `TypeError: ... reading "webContents"` (main.js:212) when a window closes during an update download. Don't just patch line 212. Design the durable workflow that keeps the app crash-free across the whole update/close lifecycle: a window-lifecycle state machine, a safe-access layer for `webContents` (respecting `isDestroyed()`), crash telemetry so this class of bug is caught before release, and a schedule/trigger that reruns the audit. Tell me what data feeds, mappings, and test machines you need, and say plainly where I'd have to change my own release workflow.

**Outside judge:** the crash-free session rate and the disappearance of this error signature in telemetry.
**Access needed:** crash-report export (Sentry/Bugsnag token) or the raw stack traces; repo read access.
**Costs you:** a change to how you release — you now gate on a lifecycle audit and a telemetry dashboard, not a one-off patch.

---

## Rung 2 — Depth: do it the way an Electron-maintainer would

**Prompt to paste:**
> Treat this as an entire class of bug, not one call site. Start from the raw evidence: the actual crash reports, the updater library source (`electron-updater` / `autoUpdater`), and Electron's window-lifecycle docs. Build (a) a state machine for window + update states, (b) an audit of *every* `webContents` / `BrowserWindow` access with the unsafe orderings enumerated (`closed`, `destroyed`, `isDestroyed()`), (c) a centralized safe-access wrapper, and (d) a deterministic failing test that reproduces the close-during-update race. Target: zero `webContents`-after-destroy derefs over a full week — an unreasonable bar you should treat as reachable via `noImplicitAny` + an ESLint rule banning raw `.webContents` outside the wrapper. Test the premise first: confirm from the traces that close-during-download is truly the root cause and not a symptom.

**Outside judge:** a Playwright/Electron integration test (`_electron.launch`) or electron-mocha spec that reproduces the race and fails before the fix, passes after; plus CI.
**Access needed:** repo + a machine that can run headless Electron (xvfb/CI runner); the crash reports.
**Costs you:** writing tests and possibly typing/ESLint cleanup across main-process files.

---

## Rung 3 — Range: the crew

Restated as verbs: *make an unreliable lifecycle reliable, reproduce a race, harden an API, prevent regressions, explain the incident.* Crew:
1. **Electron main-process engineer** — method: lifecycle state-machine audit; artefact: safe-access module + patched call sites.
2. **Reliability/SRE engineer** — method: SLO on crash-free sessions; artefact: dashboard + SLO definition.
3. **Test engineer (adversary)** — method: fault/race injection; artefact: deterministic failing regression test in CI.
4. **Concurrency/formal-methods person (adversary)** — method: interleaving enumeration; artefact: list of all unsafe close/update orderings.
5. **Incident analyst** — method: version/stack-trace correlation; artefact: confirmed root cause vs. hypothesis.

**Outside judge:** cross-check of test-engineer's repro by the formal-methods member; SRE dashboard as ground truth.
**Access needed:** repo, crash telemetry, ability to spawn 3–5 parallel workstreams.
**Costs you:** coordination — runs as parallel subagents, cheap per-agent but you own the merge.

---

## Rung 4 — Combined (altitude + depth + range)

Take Rung 1's outcome workflow, execute it with Rung 2's methods, staffed by Rung 3's crew.

**Outside judge:** the integration test *and* the week-long telemetry SLO.
**Access needed:** all of the above — crash reports, repo, CI with headless Electron, and the authority to change the release gate.
**Costs you:** the full workflow change plus parallel-agent babysitting.

---

## Recommendation
Climb to **Rung 2**. You almost certainly already have repo access today, and a single crash report is enough to start — the deterministic failing test is the fastest path to a real root cause and a permanent fix. Rung 4 is strictly better but blocked on telemetry + CI that you may not have wired up yet; if you grant those today, go straight to Rung 4. Do **not** stop at rung 0: patching line 212 with a null-guard hides the race and guarantees a recurrence.

# Ambition ladder: from "fix this crash" to "never ship a broken update"

## Rung 0 — Baseline (as asked)

> Fix the crash `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading "webContents")` at main.js:212, which fires when the user closes a window during an update download.

**Domain:** Electron main process, auto-update lifecycle. **You:** the app's developer/maintainer. **Materials:** the repo, the stack trace.

---

## Rung A — Altitude: aim at the outcome

*"And then what?"* → Fix this crash → stop this class of crash → users never get stuck in a half-updated state → releases are self-verifying and self-halting.

**Outcome:** every release is provably free of update-lifecycle crashes *before* it ships, and any that slips through is caught, symbolicated and rolled back automatically.

**Durable workflow this implies:** version-keyed crash telemetry → symbolicated stacks per release → CI gate that blocks a release on new crash signatures → staged rollout with auto-halt → post-release dashboard.

> **Prompt:** "Design and implement an update-safety pipeline for this Electron app. (1) Instrument the main process so every crash reports a symbolicated stack tagged with release version. (2) Define a crash-free-sessions SLA for the updater subsystem and a baseline from the last 30 days of telemetry. (3) Add a CI release gate that fails if update-related crash signatures regress against the prior release. (4) Configure staged rollout with automatic halt. Show the diff to the code, CI config and monitoring."
> **Judge:** the crash-free-sessions metric, and a release that a new crash signature actually blocks. **Access:** crash telemetry account (Sentry/Crashpad/Play), CI secrets, release pipeline. **Cost:** ongoing workflow change — releases now depend on telemetry being wired up.

---

## Rung D — Depth: do it like the best reliability engineer

Top practitioners don't add a null check. They treat the updater and window lifecycle as a **concurrent state machine**, find *all* races, and prove the fix with a deterministic regression test.

Depth answers:
1. **What a pro does that you didn't ask for:** model `BrowserWindow` ↔ `autoUpdater` interaction as states; audit *every* `win.webContents` / `BrowserWindow.getFocusedWindow()` call site for the same destroyed-window race; fix the pattern, not the line.
2. **Rawest material:** main-process stack traces, the `electron-updater` source, Electron window-lifecycle docs, the actual sequence of `download-progress`/`update-downloaded` events vs. `closed`.
3. **Real methods/tools:** a hand-written lifecycle state machine + unit tests; guards via `win.isDestroyed()` / `BrowserWindow.fromWebContents()` checks; a deterministic repro harness (Playwright driving Electron, or a test that programmatically closes the window mid-download against a local update server); Sentry release tagging; an ESLint rule banning bare `webContents` access.
4. **Outside judge:** a regression test that *fails on today's code* and passes after; the crash-free-session trend on real releases.

**Depth moves:** unreasonable target = *zero* crashes of this class for 30 days post-release. Test the premise: reproduce against raw event ordering, don't trust the trace. New knowledge: a race/timeline map naming every window-vs-updater interleaving that can orphan a reference.

> **Prompt:** "Treat this as a concurrency defect, not a typo. Reproduce it deterministically with a test harness that closes a BrowserWindow during an active update download. Enumerate every code path where an updater callback dereferences a window or `webContents`, and make each one safe against a destroyed window. Produce: (a) a written lifecycle/race map of window states vs. updater event order, (b) a regression test that fails on the current commit, (c) minimal patches fixing the whole pattern, (d) an ESLint rule preventing recurrence. Target: zero occurrences of this crash class in the next release."
> **Judge:** the failing→passing regression test and the ESLint rule. **Access:** repo + Node + ability to run the app headless with a local update server; ideally CI. **Cost:** hours, not minutes; needs a stubbed update server.

---

## Rung R — Range: bring in a crew

Restated as verbs: *find why a program's state goes inconsistent under concurrent user action, prove it can't, and make releases self-protecting.* Crew (run as parallel subagents):

| Member | Method | Artefact |
|---|---|---|
| Reliability engineer | Lifecycle state machine + audits | Race map + patches |
| Observability engineer | Symbolicated telemetry, crash-free-% | Dashboard + SLA baseline |
| Test automation engineer | Deterministic Electron repro harness | Regression test in CI |
| Release engineer | Canary + auto-rollback | Staged-rollout policy/logic |
| **Adversary — chaos tester** | Fuzz window actions (close/minimize/kill) mid-update | A way to *break* the conclusion; a failing case the fix must survive |

> **Prompt:** "Run the Depth task as five parallel specialists (reliability, observability, test automation, release engineering, and an adversarial chaos tester whose job is to falsify the fix). Reconcile their outputs into one change set: patches, regression test, ESLint rule, telemetry+SLA, staged rollout with halt, and a chaos test that tries to defeat it."
> **Judge:** the chaos test failing against unfixed code and the release gate hidden from the model's own code. **Access:** same as Depth plus CI + telemetry + a test update server. **Cost:** parallel compute and a real telemetry/CI budget.

---

## Rung C — Combined

> "Eliminate the update-lifecycle crash *class* and re-engineer the release process so it's verifiably safe: reproduce deterministically, fix the whole pattern, add the guard and lint rule, wire symbolicated telemetry with a crash-free SLA, gate CI on regression, and stage rollouts with auto-halt — reviewed by an adversarial chaos pass."
> **Judge:** green regression test, passing chaos test, live crash-free-session SLA. **Access:** repo, CI, telemetry, update server, release pipeline. **Cost:** a real project with a workflow change to your release process.

---

**Other axes:** speed isn't covered here (it's the default). All three axes above apply.

**Recommendation:** Do **Rung D today** — it needs only the repo, Node and a local update-server stub, and it turns a one-line patch into a pattern fix with a permanent regression test. Escalate to **Rung A/C** once you can grant CI and telemetry access; that's the rung that actually prevents the *next* update crash, not just this one.

# Ambition ladder: fix Electron update crash

**Rung 0 (as asked):** Patch the `TypeError` at `main.js:212` so the app stops throwing when a window is closed mid-update.

Below, the reference to line 212 is a symptom. The real defect is almost certainly a stale `BrowserWindow` reference surviving an `await`/event callback: the updater's `download-progress` handler (or a post-`await` continuation) captured a window, the user closed it, and the code then touches `win.webContents` on a destroyed window. Fixing the line hides one instance, not the class.

## Altitude
**Outcome:** the app stays crash-free across releases for this whole class of window-lifecycle races — not one stack trace gone, but the *recurrence* gone, and the team told automatically when a new one appears.

- **Prompt:** "Treat this crash as the first sighting of a class, not a one-off. Build the loop that keeps it fixed: (1) pull crash reports and group this error by app version, Electron version and OS to find when it started; (2) use `git bisect` (or version→commit mapping) to find the commit that introduced it; (3) map every place main-process code touches a window after an async boundary; (4) add a regression test that closes the window during an update download; (5) wire crash reporting into CI so this class is caught as a release gate, not by users."
- **Outside judge:** the crash-free-session rate in telemetry trending to zero for this error ID; the regression test failing on the old commit and passing on the new.
- **Access:** the repo + Node/Electron toolchain, your crash-reporting service (Sentry/Bugsnag/your own), and version→commit or release tags.
- **Cost to you:** you cede the "just patch it" reflex and take on a standing triage cadence; someone owns the alert.

## Depth
- **Prompt:** "Do the surgery the best Electron maintainer would, not a null-check. (1) Reproduce it deterministically: an integration test with Playwright's Electron support (or `electron-mocha`) that starts an update download and destroys the window mid-flight — get a red test before touching line 212. (2) Identify the true precondition: which async callback holds the window, and why a destroyed window is still reachable. (3) Fix at the boundary, not the call site: a guarded `sendToWindow(win, channel, ...)` helper that checks `win && !win.isDestroyed()`, and audit the whole main process for the same after-`await` pattern. (4) Migrate the touched files toward TypeScript `strict` (or a JSDoc + ESLint rule) so an unguarded `win.webContents` won't type-check. (5) Test the premise: check telemetry — is this really close-during-update, or is it any destroyed-window-then-async path? Report what the raw data says."
- **Premise tested:** "this only happens during updates" — check crash breadcrumbs for the actual user action before building a fix around the guess.
- **Unreasonable-but-reachable target:** zero occurrences of this error class across the next release on all three OSes, verified by telemetry — not "reduce it."
- **Produce new knowledge:** a lint/CI rule or typed guard that flags the anti-pattern *before* it ships, so the team learns the shape of the bug, not just this instance.
- **Outside judge:** the red-then-green regression test, TypeScript strict mode, and the crash-free-session metric on real builds.
- **Access:** repo, a local or CI machine that can run the GUI on macOS + Windows + Linux, ability to add a CI job.
- **Cost to you:** a real test harness and typed refactor of the main process; slower to land than a one-line patch.

## Range
**Verbs:** *prevent a lifecycle race from reaching users → let the team reproduce it cheaply → catch the next one automatically.* Surfaces several fields that one developer usually doesn't consult.

| Crew member | Method | Artefact |
|---|---|---|
| Concurrency/race specialist | Model the window + updater as a state machine; enumerate legal/illegal transitions | A transition table marking where a destroyed window is still referenced |
| Electron/OS systems engineer | Reproduce across OS + window-close ordering, including `beforeunload` and force-quit | OS × scenario reproduction matrix |
| Test automation engineer | Playwright-Electron integration test that closes mid-download | A deterministic failing test |
| Observability engineer | Group crashes by version/OS, set up alerting + crash-free-session SLO | Dashboard + alert rule |
| Static analysis / type-systems | Add a typed guard and a rule that forbids bare `win.webContents` after `await` | A CI check that blocks the pattern |
| **Adversary (red team)** | Try to still crash it: close during quit, during `autoUpdater.quitAndInstall`, multiple windows, tray-only window | A list of surviving repros the fix missed |

- **Prompt:** "Run the crew above in parallel, each producing its named artefact, then synthesize into one fix + one CI gate. The red-team member must find a way to still crash it or certify it can't."
- **Access / cost:** parallel subagents if available; the adversary's work is the part most teams skip and where the value is.

## Combined
- **Prompt:** "This 'cannot read webContents' crash is one instance of a window-lifecycle race. Reproduce it deterministically with a Playwright-Electron test that closes the window mid-update-download; find the introducing commit by bisect and the real precondition from crash breadcrumbs (prove or kill the 'only during updates' assumption). Fix at the boundary with a guarded send helper and audit every after-`await` window touch in the main process. Add a typed guard and a CI rule so the pattern can't type-check its way back in. Set up telemetry grouping + an alert on this error ID so the next occurrence is caught automatically. Red-team it: find a way to still crash it before declaring done. Target: zero occurrences of this class next release across macOS, Windows and Linux."
- **Outside judge / access / cost:** regression test + `tsc --strict` + crash-free-session SLO; needs the repo, all three OSes in CI, and crash-report access; costs a real refactor and a standing alert owner.

**Recommendation:** take the **Depth** rung today — it needs only the repo and a test environment, and it converts one patched line into a regression test, a guarded boundary, and a static check. To unlock the **Combined** rung, the first ask is crash-report access (Sentry/Bugsnag/your own) plus a CI matrix on all three OSes; that's what turns "fixed this crash" into "this crash can't come back unnoticed."

## Ambition ladder: Electron crash on window close during update

**Rung 0 (as asked):** Guard the `webContents` access at main.js:212 so closing a window during an update download no longer throws.

That's a patch. It fixes tonight's stack trace and leaves the class of bug alive. The interesting question is what's above it.

---

### Altitude

**Outcome (checkable):** No unhandled main-process exceptions from window/update lifecycle races ship to users — measured as zero new Sentry groups for that failure class, release over release. Not "fix this crash," but "the app stops generating this family of crashes."

Climbing: fix the crash → users stop hitting error dialogs/lost state → updates stop being scary → *the app stays crash-free across releases, without me triaging each stack trace by hand.*

The durable version of this is a loop, not a PR:
- **Inputs:** crash reports keyed to app version and Electron version.
- **Mappings:** version → commit, source maps, owner of the affected module.
- **Verification:** a repro harness that replays window/update lifecycles on each target OS.
- **Cadence:** new crash group → auto-repro → candidate fix + regression test → PR for review.

- **Prompt:** "Our main process throws `webContents` undefined errors when window lifecycle overlaps async update downloads. Build the loop that keeps this class of crash at zero: (1) pull the crash groups for the last 3 releases, de-minified; (2) build a Playwright/puppeteer-electron harness that races window-close against `autoUpdater` download states and reproduces the throw; (3) fix the root cause class, not line 212; (4) add the repro as a CI regression test. Report each crash group, its repro status, and the fix."
- **Outside judge:** the repro harness (fails before, passes after) plus a quiet period in the crash feed.
- **Access:** crash reporting (e.g. Sentry) API, source maps, a CI runner for Electron, per-OS test machines.
- **Cost to you:** standing up CI repro + giving the model crash-feed credentials; you review PRs instead of writing patches.

### Depth

- **Pro move not asked for:** treat line 212 as a *symptom*. Audit every place `webContents`, `BrowserWindow`, or window refs are touched after an `await`, and prove which are racy.
- **Rawest material:** the actual crash events with environment metadata and source-mapped stacks — not the single line you pasted.
- **Methods/instruments:** Electron lifecycle semantics (`isDestroyed()`, `closed`/`close` events, `destroy()` timing), a lifecycle fuzzer that permutes close/download/quit orderings, static analysis or an ESLint rule banning bare `.webContents` access in async paths, and a canary release.
- **Unreasonable target, framed as reachable:** *"Eliminate the entire undefined-window-reference class across the main process; the fuzzer should find nothing in 10,000 permutations."*
- **Premise tested:** "the update download is what makes it crash" — maybe it's any in-flight IPC, and updates are just correlated.
- **Produce new knowledge:** fuzz the lifecycle, find every still-reachable failure, validate fixes against permutations the fix wasn't written for.
- **Outside judge:** the fuzzer + a held-back set of permutations + CI.
- **Prompt:** "Do a lifecycle-race audit of the main process. Load the raw crash events (not summaries). Build a fuzzer over {window close, update download/apply, app quit, IPC in-flight} orderings and record all throws. Fix every reachable undefined-reference, not just 212. Add a lint rule against unguarded post-await window access. Target: 10k permutations, zero unhandled throws." 
- **Access:** the event export, a machine able to run and fuzz Electron headless.
- **Cost to you:** an afternoon wiring the fuzzer and a decision to enforce the lint rule on the team.

### Range

**Verbs:** "a crash fix" → *prevent a whole class of async-lifecycle failures; let anyone reproduce it cheaply; prove the fix holds under permutations.*

| Crew member | Method | Artefact |
|---|---|---|
| Concurrency specialist | Model the race, enumerate async gaps and interleavings | Race map + list of unsafe windows |
| Fuzzer / chaos engineer | Permute lifecycle orderings, record throws | Fuzz report: N permutations, M failures |
| Static-analysis engineer | Scan for unguarded window/`webContents` access post-await | Lint rule + findings list |
| Release/incident engineer | Canary the fix, watch crash rate per version | Rollout + crash-rate delta |
| **Red-teamer** (adversary) | Try to still crash it after the fix; hunt for the metric flattering the patch | Counterexamples or a clean bill |

The levers you were leaving on the table:

- **Ask what data to pull.** You get the follow-up work scoped for you.
- **Name the audience and the stakes** (skeptical execs, a board, a budget decision) — it changes everything downstream.

5. **Use the launches as evidence.** Right now they're trivia. Either they're the retention medicine (show it) or they're a distraction from the real problem (say so).

Your prompt treats the survey as a summarization task. It's actually a prioritization task, and summarization is the weakest possible way to use 1,400 opinions.

The tell is "top 5 themes." That framing (a) throws away magnitude, (b) hides segment differences, (c) has no connection to any decision, and (d) gives you no way to check whether it's right.

Ask for this instead:

**1. Structure, not prose.** Have it classify every response as a labeled dataset: response ID, one or more themes, sentiment, the segment the respondent belongs to. Then any theme count is a query you can run, not an assertion you have to trust.

**2. Segment the themes.** A theme across all 1,400 is nearly useless. Which themes concentrate in which cohort — plan tier, tenure, churned vs. renewed, high vs. low NPS? "Enterprise admins care about X; self-serve users care about Y" is a decision; "X and Y are top themes" is trivia.

**3. Quantify and trend.** Prevalence (% of respondents, not raw mentions), sentiment skew, and change vs. last year's survey if you have it. A theme that's loud but shrinking is a different decision than one that's quiet but doubling.

**4. Tie it to outcomes.** Which themes actually correlate with churn, renewal, or expansion? Weight themes by business impact, not volume. The most-mentioned complaint is often not the one costing you money.

**5. Finish at decisions.** Not "here are 5 themes" but "here are the 3 things worth doing, ranked, each with the evidence for it, the strongest counter-evidence, and what would have to be true."

**6. Make it auditable.** Representative verbatims with response IDs so a human can spot-check, an explicit statement of what was ambiguous or double-counted, and a section on what you expected to hear but didn't.

**7. Keep it interrogable.** Ask it to flag its own weak spots and answer follow-ups against the same structured data, rather than regenerating an answer from scratch.

A tighter version of the actual request:

> Classify all 1,400 responses into a structured dataset with response ID, themes (multi-label), sentiment, and respondent segment. Then tell me: which themes concentrate in which segments, how each theme's prevalence and sentiment compare to last year, and which themes correlate most with churn or renewal. End with the 3 highest-impact actions, ranked, each with its supporting evidence, its strongest counter-argument, and the assumption that would flip the ranking. Include representative verbatims with IDs and a list of ambiguities you had to resolve.

One line summary: stop asking "what are the themes" and start asking "what should we do, for whom, and how confident are you."

Instead of collapsing 1,400 voices into one tidy ranked list, ask for something you can act on and trust:

**Reframe around decisions, not themes.** Themes are an output; what you actually want is "what should we change, and how confident should we be?"

A stronger ask:

> "Analyze all 1,400 free-text responses. Segment them (by cohort, product line, tenure, NPS bucket — whatever dimensions exist in the survey). For each segment, surface the dominant themes with supporting verbatim quotes and counts. Identify: (1) themes where segments disagree — where one group's delight is another's pain; (2) low-frequency/high-severity issues that raw ranking would bury; (3) themes that have changed in sentiment versus prior surveys if available. Flag contradictions and themes you're uncertain about because the evidence is thin. End with the 3–5 changes most likely to move the needle, each tied to the evidence, with a confidence level and the counterargument against it."

Why this is more ambitious:

- **Segmentation beats aggregation.** "Top 5 themes across everyone" averages away the disagreement that's usually the real finding.
- **Frequency ≠ importance.** A ranked list hides the rare, severe, churn-driving complaint. Ask explicitly for both.
- **Quantify the text.** Parallel coding (themes + counts + sentiment + severity) turns opinion into a scoreboard you can defend.
- **Force uncertainty into the open.** Ask for confidence levels and thin-evidence flags, so you know what not to over-trust.
- **Demand falsifiability.** "Give the strongest counterargument to each conclusion" is what separates analysis from a plausible-sounding summary.

If you want to push further: ask it to produce a reusable codebook (theme definitions + example quotes) that a second pass — or a second model — can apply to *new* responses next quarter, so you're building a repeatable instrument, not a one-off answer.

Don't ask for a summary. A summary compresses 1,400 voices into 5 labels and throws away everything that makes them useful — who said what, how strongly, what changed, and what to do about it. Ask for a decision instead.

A better prompt:

> "Read all 1,400 free-text responses. For each, extract: sentiment, the specific product/feature/policy mentioned, and whether it's an ask, a complaint, or praise. Group them into themes, and for each theme tell me: how many respondents, how it skews across customer segments (plan, tenure, region), and the 2–3 verbatim quotes that best capture it. Then rank the themes by (volume × severity × how fixable they are), and for the top 3 give me a concrete recommended action and what evidence would confirm it. Flag any theme that's growing, any segment that's disproportionately unhappy, and any low-volume / high-severity issue that a simple count would bury."

Why this is more ambitious:

- **Segmented, not just counted.** "1,400 people mentioned pricing" is useless if it's all one plan tier. Tied to segments, it's a business decision.
- **Ranked by impact, not volume.** The loudest theme is rarely the most important. Severity and fixability change the priority.
- **Preserves the signal of the tail.** Top-5 summaries systematically hide the niche, high-severity complaint (the one churn reason) and the emerging theme.
- **Ends in action.** It asks for a recommendation and a falsification test, so the output drives the next meeting rather than decorating a slide.
- **Traceable.** Quotes and counts let you verify the model didn't hallucinate a theme — critical with LLM summarization over 1,400 docs.

If you want to push further: have it also produce the per-response structured table as an intermediate artifact, so both the counts and the themes are auditable. The summary is the cheap part; the structured extraction underneath it is what you can actually trust and re-slice.

Your prompt asks for tests of a module. The ambitious version asks for a verified specification of the module's behavior under adversarial conditions — with bugs found, not just coverage added. Test-writing is a means; here the ends are correctness of money math and confidence at the boundaries.

**What to ask instead:**

> Treat `billing/invoice.py` as a black box with a well-defined contract. First, derive and write down the invariants that must hold for any correct prorated invoice (e.g. line items sum to the invoice total; total is never negative unless a credit applies; proration fractions sum to 1 across a plan-change pair; rounding never invents or destroys cents at the batch level). Then attack the module at its boundaries: plan changes mid-cycle, upgrades vs downgrades, same-day start/end, mid-period cancellations, trials, credits/refunds, zero-dollar and free→paid transitions, timezone/DST and leap-year month lengths, and currency rounding. Use property-based tests (Hypothesis) to fuzz inputs against the invariants, plus targeted example tests for each boundary. Every time an invariant fails, report it as a candidate bug with a minimal reproducer rather than encoding the buggy behavior as the expected result. Deliver: the invariant list, the test suite, and a written list of suspected defects with severity and repro.

**The axes you're buying:**
- **From coverage to correctness** — invariants and properties, not just line coverage.
- **From arrangement to attack** — actively trying to break it, especially money/rounding.
- **From tests to a spec** — writing down the contract makes the module's ambiguity visible.
- **From green to findings** — bugs surfaced as the deliverable, not passing tests.

**Highest-leverage specifics for this domain:** rounding and penny allocation across line items, timezone/DST correctness, and the upgrade/downgrade-with-credit path. Those are where proration code actually breaks.

**One caution:** if you don't have a trusted oracle (past invoices, a reference implementation, Finance's rules), state that up front. Otherwise the model may codify plausible-but-wrong behavior. Tell it what "correct" is anchored to.

Your original ask treats "write unit tests" as the goal. Testing is a means; the goal is *confidence that invoices are correct*. Rewrite the ask around that:

**Reframe the objective**
> "Make our prorated-invoice computation provably correct and hard to break. Start by characterizing exactly what `billing/invoice.py` is supposed to do for plan changes — including the edge cases we haven't specified — then build a testing strategy around it."

The key move: don't hand over a file and a verb. Hand over *the property you want guaranteed* (money is never miscomputed) and let the model figure out the surface area.

**What the ambitious version asks for instead**

1. **A behavioral spec before any test.** Ask the model to write down the invoicing rules it infers (mid-cycle upgrades, downgrades, credits, timezone/day-count conventions, rounding, fractional cents, leap months), flag every ambiguity, and get those resolved — because most billing bugs are unspecified-behavior bugs, not code bugs.

2. **Property-based tests over example-based ones.** Proration has invariants worth encoding:
   - Parts sum to the whole (prorated pieces across a cycle sum to the full-cycle amount).
   - Upgrade-then-downgrade within one cycle nets to the marginal difference, not double-billing.
   - Credits are conserved: nothing created or destroyed by splitting a period.
   - Rounding never silently loses or invents cents.
   Ask for Hypothesis (or equivalent) strategies that generate random plan changes and assert these, not just a handful of hand-picked examples.

3. **Boundary and adversarial cases explicitly.** Day 0, last day of cycle, exact-midpoint, zero-price plans, negative proration, currency rounding (e.g. JPY 0-decimal), DST/timezone shifts, plan changes that cancel each other, refunds and trials overlapping the switch.

4. **Test the integration, not just the unit.** The riskiest bugs live at the seams — how `invoice.py` gets used by the billing run, ledger writes, idempotency when a job reruns, retries. Ask for characterization tests against the real calling path, plus a golden-file/approval test of full invoice outputs so future refactors get caught.

5. **Make it a regression harness, not a one-off.** Ask for fixtures/builders that make *future* proration scenarios cheap to add, a documented list of known-tricky cases, and mutation-testing (mutmut/cosmic-ray) run against the module so you learn whether the tests would actually catch a bug.

**The single best rewrite**
> "Build a correctness strategy for prorated plan-change invoicing. First infer and document the intended rules from `billing/invoice.py` and flag every ambiguity. Then deliver: property-based tests for the invariants (pieces sum to whole, upgrade→downgrade nets to the difference, credits conserved, no lost cents), a fixture harness so new scenarios are cheap, integration tests against the real billing-call path including reruns/idempotency, and a mutation-testing pass to prove the tests have teeth. Tell me what you *can't* guarantee."

Same effort, but you walk away with a spec, a reusable harness, and real confidence — not 12 unit tests that all pass because they assert the current code's behavior back at itself.

Your current ask treats testing as a coverage chore: it will mock every dependency, assert the code does whatever it currently does (bugs included), and tell you nothing about whether proration is *correct*.

Proration is a great place to aim higher because it has real invariants and an independent oracle. The ambitious version tests the *contract*, not the implementation.

What to reach for:

- **Property-based over example-based.** Use Hypothesis. State invariants: total equals the integral of usage × rate; intervals never overlap or leave gaps; an upgrade-then-downgrade nets to usage at each rate; no zero-length-period double charge; monotonicity (a longer period costs at least as much at the same rate). Generate random timelines, plan changes, and price tables.
- **An oracle / differential test.** Compute the invoice a second, independent way (a from-scratch reference model, or compare against a known spec like Stripe's proration rules) and assert agreement. Tests against a re-implementation catch bugs that tests against the code itself cannot.
- **Time is the hard part.** Inject a clock; test DST transitions, month boundaries (28/29/30/31 days), leap years, changes landing exactly on a boundary, and sub-second/partial-day rounding.
- **Money edges.** Currency rounding modes, half-cents, negative credits for downgrades, zero-dollar plans, very large and NaN/infinity inputs.
- **Integration, not just unit.** A sequence of plan changes over a billing cycle producing one coherent invoice, plus a golden corpus of real or realistic scenarios as regression anchors.
- **Then measure quality.** Gate on mutation testing (mutmut/cosmic-ray) so you know the suite actually detects faults, not that it just executes lines.
- **Ask it to find bugs, not pass.** Explicitly request a findings report of suspected defects with repros, and permission to flag the current behavior as wrong rather than enshrining it.

A prompt that captures this:

> Treat `billing/invoice.py` as a specification to be verified. First, model proration explicitly: invoice as a pure function of (usage intervals, price schedule, clock). Refactor toward that if needed. Then build a test suite that (1) uses Hypothesis to assert invariants — conservation of total, non-overlapping complete intervals, monotonicity, correct netting across multiple plan changes; (2) uses a second, independent reference implementation as a differential oracle; (3) covers timezone/DST, month-length, leap-year, rounding, currency, and negative-credit edges; (4) includes a golden-scenario regression corpus. Add a mutation-testing run and report the score. Finally, produce a findings report of any suspected bugs or under-specified behavior, with minimal repros, and tell me which current outputs look wrong rather than locking them in. Prioritize catching defects over coverage percentage.

That turns one afternoon of line-covering into a correctness argument you can actually trust before money moves.

- A Python environment where you can install packages.
- Access to plan-change events + processor invoice records (connector, export, or API key).
- The proration spec / contract rule you're testing against.
- The outside judge (reconciliation script / processor query) exposed as something the model can actually run.

## Recommendation

**Start at Rung 2.** It needs only the code and a Python env you already have, and it replaces "write some unit tests" with a proof plus a mutation score — the biggest ambition jump per unit of access. If you can hand over invoice history and processor access today, go to **Rung 1** (adds the durability) or **Rung 3** (adds the adversary), which are where the *real* bugs usually hide. Rung 2 alone is the highest rung whose prerequisites you can almost certainly supply right now.

One caution: don't let the ladder drift up to "grow revenue" — it turns abstract and unverifiable. "No wrong invoice on a plan change" is the right ceiling.

## Rung 1 — Altitude (aim at the outcome)

**And then what?** Tests pass → the proration code is correct → customers get correct charges → no billing disputes, no refunds, no revenue leakage. Your request keeps coming back every time there's a proration bug, which is the signal you want the *outcome*, not the task.

**Prompt:**

> Build a durable billing-correctness harness for our proration logic, not one-off tests. Produce (a) an executable spec of what correct proration means across every plan-change sequence (upgrade, downgrade, mid-cycle, quantity change, trial→paid, coupons, credits), and (b) an automated suite that gates every future change to `billing/invoice.py` in CI. Wire it so a proration regression fails the build before it can reach a customer invoice, and write the runbook for maintaining it. Target outcome: zero proration-driven disputes or leakage going forward.

- **Judge:** the CI gate (pass/fail on every PR) + the trend in proration-attributable refunds/disputes.
- **Access:** CI config, plan/pricing schema, billing event schema.
- **Cost:** workflow change — tests become a merge gate; ongoing maintenance. Days, not hours.

## Rung 2 — Depth (do it like a payments team)

Four answers: (1) a top billing engineer treats money math as a *spec* problem — reference implementation + properties + differential + mutation testing, not example tests. (2) Rawest material: the pricing config, real plan-change event logs, and processor-side invoices as ground truth. (3) Instruments: **Hypothesis** (property-based), a naive **integer-minor-unit reference model**, **freezegun** (month/DST boundaries), **mutmut** (mutation testing), differential testing. (4) Outside judge: mutation kill-rate, differential disagreement count, and a finance/payments domain expert signing the spec.

**Prompt:**

> Do proration correctness the way a payments-infrastructure team would. Start from raw inputs: the plan/pricing config, real plan-change event logs, and processor-side invoices as ground truth where available. Build (1) a deliberately naive but obviously-correct reference implementation of proration in integer minor units; (2) a Hypothesis property suite asserting the money invariants — allocation sums exactly to total, no lost or gained cents, monotonicity across upgrade/downgrade, idempotency, currency and rounding rules, DST and month-boundary handling; (3) differential tests comparing `invoice.py` to the reference over millions of randomized event sequences; (4) mutation testing to prove the suite actually bites. Target: mutation kill-rate ≥ 95% and zero differential disagreements over 10^6 sequences. Report every invariant violation as a reproducible bug report — expect this to find real bugs in the module, not just characterize it.

- **Judge:** mutmut kill-rate; differential disagreement count; domain-expert sign-off on the spec.
- **Access:** install `hypothesis`, `mutmut`, `freezegun`; read access to pricing config + a billing event sample.
- **Cost:** reference-model and spec work; someone who knows the billing rules. This changes the module, not just its tests.

**Depth moves applied:** unreasonable-but-reachable target (≥95% kill-rate, 10^6 sequences, not "tests pass"); test the premise first (does it even use integer cents / Decimal, or floats?); produce new knowledge (a found-bug + leakage report you don't have today).

Third, build a CI-runnable verification harness — property-based tests, an independent oracle, and the history as a golden regression set — that would have caught each discrepancy."
- **Outside judge:** the historical golden corpus (the module must reproduce past invoices or explain why not) and the CI harness itself.

Your prompt describes a symptom, not a problem. `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading "webContents")` on line 212 is almost certainly a lifecycle race: something captured a `BrowserWindow` (or its `webContents`) reference, then used it in an async continuation after the user closed the window and Electron tore the object down. Asking for "fix line 212" gets you a `if (win && !win.isDestroyed())` guard around one call site — and the identical bug will fire again next week from a different callback. Here's how to aim higher.

## What the narrow ask misses

- **It fixes one instance of a class.** Any code path that touches a window after an `await`, an `autoUpdater` event, a `setTimeout`, or an IPC round-trip can hit this. Line 212 is where it *crashed*, not where the design is wrong.
- **It hides the race instead of resolving it.** A null check at the crash site converts "crash" into "silently dropped update notification" — which is a worse user experience and harder to debug.
- **It ignores ownership.** Nothing in the ask forces a decision about *who owns window references* and *when they are valid*. That's the actual architectural question.
- **It skips verification.** "Fixed" with no reproduction test means the race can regress invisibly.
- **It ignores the update flow itself.** The fact that an async update download outlives its window is a product-level design gap, not just a null-check gap.

## The reframe

The real request is: *"Make window/WebContents access safe across the whole app by construction, prove the update-close race is gone, and leave a mechanism that prevents this class of bug from recurring."* That's bigger but far more valuable.

## A better prompt to hand the model

> We crashed with `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading "webContents")` in main.js:212 when the user closed a window during an update download. Treat this as a symptom of a lifecycle/ownership bug, not a line-level defect.
>
> 1. Root-cause it. Trace every path where a `BrowserWindow` or its `webContents` is referenced after an async boundary. Explain the exact interleaving that produces the crash, including which `autoUpdater`/download event fires after `'closed'`.
> 2. Audit the whole main process for the same class of bug — any window reference used after `await`, event handler, or timer. Give me a ranked list with file:line and the triggering interleaving for each, not just the one on line 212.
> 3. Propose a single ownership model: one place that owns live windows and mediates all access. Show the interface. I want a design where a stale reference is impossible to use, not one that relies on defensive checks scattered everywhere.
> 4. Make the update flow itself robust — what should happen to an in-flight download when its window closes? Cancellation, reassignment, or completion-without-UI? Recommend and implement.
> 5. Add a deterministic regression test that reproduces close-during-download. If it can't be made deterministic, tell me why and what refactor would make it so.
> 6. Add a guardrail so this can't silently return: a lint rule, a type wrapper that makes raw `.webContents` access awkward, or an ESLint/TS constraint. Explain the tradeoff.
> 7. Improve observability: does our crash reporting capture the window state and update phase at the moment of failure? If not, add it.
>
> Show your reasoning at each step. Prefer the smallest change that makes the *class* of bug impossible, and call out anything you're deliberately not doing.

## Why this is the more ambitious ask

It moves the model across four levels at once. **Depth:** from one line to the mechanism. **Breadth:** from one call site to every async window touch in the main process. **Prevention:** from a patch to an ownership model plus a test plus a lint/type guardrail. **Product:** from "don't crash" to "what should an update do when its window dies?" Each is independently valuable; together they turn a one-off fix into a durable repair.

## Two calibration notes

First, ask the model to *show the interleaving* rather than assert a cause. Race-condition diagnoses are easy to get plausible-and-wrong; the event ordering is the falsifiable part. Second, tell it to give you the ranked audit *before* it edits, so you can scope the blast radius. A full-app lifecycle refactor is exactly the kind of "ambitious" that can balloon; you want to choose consciously between the guardrail-only fix (cheap, still correct) and the ownership-model fix (more invasive, genuinely prevents recurrence).

Finally, keep the original constraint explicit: the user-visible behavior must not regress — a closed window should still not crash, *and* an open window should still get its update prompt. "Fix the crash" without that clause invites a fix that just swallows the race.

You're asking for a line fix. The crash is a symptom, and the narrow prompt locks the model into patching the symptom — a null check at line 212 — which will leave the same class of bug everywhere else in the update flow. Here's how to reframe it.

## What the error actually tells you

`Cannot read properties of undefined (reading "webContents")` means the *window reference itself* is `undefined`, not merely destroyed. That distinction matters. A destroyed `BrowserWindow` still exists as an object (`.isDestroyed()` returns true); an `undefined` one means the variable was nulled on close, a `Map.get(id)` missed, a `WeakRef` was collected, or a getter returned nothing — and then a stale async callback (almost certainly `autoUpdater.on('download-progress' | 'update-downloaded' | 'error', ...)`) fired against it. So the real questions are: *which* reference went undefined, *why does a callback outlive its window*, and *how many other callbacks share that path*. A guard at 212 answers none of them.

## What to ask for instead

**1. Root cause and a reproduction, before any fix.** Ask the model to trace the exact async path that reaches line 212, identify every window reference the update flow touches, and produce a minimal repro (close the window mid-download). A guard written without this is guesswork.

**2. A systemic fix, not a null check.** Ask for a single window-access abstraction — e.g. a helper that resolves a live window via `BrowserWindow.fromWebContents` or `win.isDestroyed()`, returning `null` when dead — and to route *all* main-process sends through it. One place that decides whether a window is usable beats twenty `if (win)` sprinkles.

**3. Decouple the updater from windows entirely.** The autoUpdater should be a service that emits events; each window subscribes on creation and unsubscribes on `'closed'`. Downloads should never hold a window reference at all — they should continue or abort based on a product decision, not on UI presence.

**4. Audit the whole class.** Ask it to grep the main process for every dereference of possibly-destroyed objects: `webContents.send`, `dialog.showMessageBox(parent)`, tray icons, `event.sender` in IPC handlers, and the other update callbacks (`checking-for-update`, `update-available`, `quitAndInstall`). The close-during-download path is one instance; the refactor should cover them.

**5. Tests that would have caught it.** Ask for a regression test that simulates window close during an update download (Playwright/Spectron or a unit test with a fake window registry), plus tests asserting the guard returns `null` instead of throwing. Require the suite to pass *and* fail against the old code.

**6. A product answer, not just a crash fix.** What *should* happen when the user closes the window mid-download? On macOS the app stays alive after the last window closes; on Windows it may quit entirely. Ask the model to state intended behavior (download continues to tray? notification on completion?) and implement toward it — correctness plus UX.

**7. Guardrails so it doesn't recur.** Ask for TypeScript types that make a live window non-optional, or an ESLint rule banning direct `.webContents` access in the main process. Plus a two-paragraph postmortem: what the invariant is, who owns window references, and when they're invalidated.

## Paste-ready replacement prompt

> In this Electron app, fix `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading "webContents")` at main.js:212, hit when a window closes during an update download — but treat it as a lifecycle bug, not a line bug.
>
> First, find the root cause: reproduce the crash (close the window mid-download), trace the exact async callback that reaches line 212, and identify why the window reference is `undefined` rather than merely destroyed. Report the full trace before changing code.
>
> Then fix the class, not the instance: introduce one window-access abstraction that returns `null` for destroyed/undefined windows and route all main-process `webContents` access through it. Decouple the autoUpdater from windows — it should emit events that windows subscribe to on creation and unsubscribe from on `'closed'`, so a download never holds a window reference. Audit the rest of the main process for the same stale-reference pattern (tray, dialogs, IPC `event.sender`, other autoUpdater events) and fix those too.
>
> Add a regression test that closes the window during a download and asserts no crash; confirm the test fails on the current code. State the intended behavior when a window closes mid-download (continue in background, notify, or abort) and implement it. Add guardrails — types or a lint rule preventing raw `.webContents` access. Finish with a short postmortem covering the invariant and ownership of window references, and list any other risks you found.

That prompt gets you a fix, a repro, coverage of the bug class, tests, a product decision, and guardrails — instead of one guarded line.

Your prompt is a scalp-stitch where the patient needs a diagnosis. It names one line, one symptom, one scenario, and asks for the smallest change that makes the error stop printing. A capable model will hand you `if (win && !win.isDestroyed())` at line 212, you'll patch it, and the identical crash will resurface three functions over next week. Here's why that framing is weak, and how to escalate it.

**What's wrong with the narrow version.** First, it treats a lifecycle race as a typo. `Cannot read properties of undefined (reading "webContents")` at an update-download progress callback almost always means code is holding a reference to a `BrowserWindow` across an async boundary and touching it after teardown. The line is a symptom; the disease is an ownership model where nobody owns window lifetime. Second, it fixes exactly one call site. If one callback dereferences a stale window, others do too — every `webContents.send`, every progress emitter, every `dialog.showMessageBox(win, …)`. Third, it encodes no decision about intended behavior. When a user closes the window mid-download, what *should* happen? Cancel the download? Let it finish in a tray-resident process? Prompt them? The bug exists largely because that question was never answered. Fourth, it demands no proof. You get a patch with no regression test, no audit, and no guardrail, so nothing prevents recurrence.

**Dimensions of ambition.** Push the request along several axes at once:

- *Root cause, not site.* Ask the model to find every place a window reference (or `webContents`, or `win.id`-derived lookup) is captured and used after an `await`, an event handler, or a timer callback — then fix the class.
- *Architecture.* Reframe from "guard every access" to "make the unsafe state unrepresentable." A window registry module that owns lifecycle, hands out `isDestroyed`-checked accessors, and broadcasts only to live windows turns dozens of scattered guards into one deep module. The update subsystem in particular should not hold a window reference at all: it should emit state changes on an event bus (`updating:progress`, `updating:ready`) and let whichever UI is currently alive subscribe.
- *Behavioral spec.* Force the intended UX into the prompt. Closing during download, quitting during download, reloading during an IPC round-trip, main window closed but tray still running — enumerate the teardown matrix and state what each should do.
- *Determinism.* Demand a failing test first. This race is usually timing-dependent, so ask for an injected clock or fake timers and a deterministic reproduction (open window, start download, close window at a controlled point, assert no throw and the correct post-condition).
- *Observability.* If this reached a user, your crash reporting failed too. Ask for structured error capture around window/IPC boundaries so the next instance reports itself.
- *Prevention.* TypeScript strict null checks, an ESLint rule banning raw `win.webContents` outside the registry, and a `safeSend(win, channel, payload)` helper that makes the dangerous pattern hard to write.

**A paste-ready prompt.**

> We have a lifecycle crash in our Electron main process: `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading "webContents")` at main.js:212, triggered when a user closes a window during an update download. Don't just patch line 212. Instead:
> 1. Find the root cause by auditing every place we hold a `BrowserWindow`/`webContents` reference across an `await`, timer, or event callback, and summarize the failure mode.
> 2. Propose a design where window lifetime is owned in one module — a registry that provides safe accessors and a broadcast-to-live-windows API — and where the update subsystem emits events instead of referencing windows directly.
> 3. Write down the intended behavior for closing during download, quitting during download, reloading during IPC, and window-closed-but-tray-running. Flag any you need a product decision on.
> 4. Implement the design, starting with a deterministic failing test that reproduces this exact race using fake timers.
> 5. Add guardrails: a `safeSend` helper, a lint rule or type constraint preventing raw dereference elsewhere, and error capture at window/IPC boundaries.
> Give me a short written plan before you change code, and tell me what you're uncertain about.

**If you want a lighter version**, collapse it to: "This is a symptom of unsafe window-reference handling. Audit all such sites, propose a minimal ownership fix, define intended teardown behavior, and prove it with a regression test."

The core shift: ask for the *class*, the *cause*, the *decision*, and the *proof* — not the line. That turns a five-minute patch into a durable fix, and a good model will happily meet the higher bar.

Something like:

> Our product dashboard loads in ~6s (measured at p50/p75 for real users in production, not localhost). Stack: [framework, DB, hosting, auth/API layer]. Make it fast.
>
> Start by profiling rather than guessing: identify where the 6s actually goes (server render, DB queries, waterfall of API calls, JS bundle parse/hydration, third-party scripts, network). Give me a breakdown with evidence, not a list of plausible causes.
>
> Then give me a ranked fix list scored on measured impact, effort, and risk, with a target number ("get p75 under 2s"). For each fix, name the metric it moves and how we'd verify it. Tell me which ones you'd reject and why.
>
> Then implement the highest-leverage fix end to end, show the before/after numbers, and tell me what to measure next.

What changed, and why it matters:
- **Measure, don't guess** — "6 seconds" alone is unfalsifiable; ask where the time goes and force evidence.
- **Define "faster"** — a target SLO (p75 < 2s) turns opinions into a pass/fail.
- **Rank by impact/effort/risk** — prevents a flat list of 20 generic suggestions.
- **Ask what to reject** — the most useful senior signal is often "don't do this."
- **Require implementation + before/after** — turns advice into a verified result.

If you can't hand it production data, say so explicitly and have it tell you exactly what to instrument first — that's the actual first step.

The current ask has three quiet limits: **"suggest"** invites a generic listicle, **"faster"** has no target so it can't be verified, and the model has zero evidence — no code, no profile, no numbers — so it can only guess.

Ask it to **diagnose and decide**, not opine. Something like:

> Our product dashboard's LCP is ~6s. Target: under 1.5s on a mid-tier laptop over fast 3G.
>
> Context — [stack + versions], the page's entry component, the network waterfall, a CPU profile of the load, and the top 5 dependencies by bundle size are attached.
>
> Load them and tell me **where the time actually goes**: network vs. JS parse/exec vs. render/paint vs. API latency vs. serial request chains. Give me a diagnosis backed by the evidence, not a checklist.
>
> Then rank fixes by (impact × confidence) / effort, split them into quick wins vs. re-architecture, flag anything that risks correctness or SEO, and tell me exactly how to measure that each fix worked. Be specific to this code — no advice like "use a CDN."

The upgrades, in short:

- **Set a target and an environment.** "Faster" → "LCP < 1.5s on X." Now it's pass/fail.
- **Feed it evidence.** Profile + waterfall + entry component. You go from generic tips to a real diagnosis; without data the model can only pattern-match.
- **Change the verb.** "Suggest" → "diagnose, rank, and plan." You get an engineer's triage instead of a blog post.
- **Make it falsifiable.** Ask for the measurement method so you can confirm each fix actually landed.

Your ask treats the deck as a container for three facts. That's why it will produce something generic: you've handed over symptoms and asked for formatting, so the model will pad, invent connective tissue, and generate slides that say "revenue was flat" without ever saying what anyone should *do*. A QBR is not a status report. It's an argument about the next quarter, delivered to people who control resources. The goal isn't slides — it's a decision.

So the ambitious move is to stop asking for an artifact and start asking for thinking, with the deck as the output of that thinking. Here's how to reframe.

**1. Name the audience and the room.** A board, a peer leadership team, and a skeptical CFO all want different things. "QBR deck" tells the model nothing. "A deck to convince our executives to reallocate Q3 spend toward retention" tells it everything — tone, what to foreground, what to cut.

**2. Force a thesis.** Flat revenue plus churn rising from 3.1% to 3.8% monthly plus two feature launches is not neutral data. It has a shape: growth has stalled while the bucket is leaking, and the features you shipped didn't fix it. That's a story. Ask the model to find and defend the sharpest honest version of it, then structure the deck around a single-sentence headline.

**3. Demand causation, not correlation.** Require it to propose the most likely *why* behind the churn uptick and then tell you what data would confirm or kill that theory. This converts the deck from "here are the numbers" into "here's our diagnosis and confidence level."

**4. Make it forecast, not just report.** A backward-looking QBR is a museum. Ask for the trajectory: if 3.8% churn holds, what happens to net revenue next quarter and the one after? When does flat become declining? Executives fund futures, not pasts.

**5. Ask for the decisions.** Every good QBR ends with "we need X." Ask the model to state explicitly which decisions you want, what each costs, and what happens if they say no.

**6. Pre-load the cross-examination.** Have it generate the three hardest questions the room will ask — especially "why should we believe the features aren't working, and when will you know?" — with tight answers.

Here's a prompt you could paste, keeping your actual numbers:

> You're a strategy partner helping me build a QBR deck for [audience] whose purpose is [the decision you want]. Use only the data below; if something is missing, flag it explicitly rather than inventing it. Data: revenue flat QoQ; monthly churn rose from 3.1% to 3.8%; we launched two features (X and Y).
>
> Before writing any slides: (a) give me the sharpest honest one-sentence headline, (b) diagnose the most likely cause of the churn rise and the data that would confirm it, (c) tell me what these three facts together imply about next quarter if nothing changes, (d) list the gaps you'd need filled to be confident.
>
> Then produce a 6-slide narrative arc: headline, diagnosis, evidence, trajectory, plan, ask. For each slide give the key takeaway, the supporting point, and any chart I should include. Finish with the three toughest questions from this audience and my answers, plus a list of the decisions I'm requesting and their tradeoffs.

Notice what this does: it makes the model earn every slide, forbids fabrication, and puts the *decisions* at the center. It also front-loads reasoning so the deck is derivative rather than decorative.

A few optional upgrades depending on how far you want to push:

- **Ask for a pre-mortem.** "It's three months later and this plan failed — what were the two most likely reasons?" This surfaces risk before the room does.
- **Ask for the counter-narrative.** "Write the strongest case that churn is fine and this is noise." If it can't make that case, you'll present with more conviction.
- **Ask for a one-slide version and a ten-slide version.** Forcing compression tests whether there's a real spine.
- **Ask for the email you'd send instead of the deck.** Sometimes the whole argument fits in five sentences, and the deck is theater.

The deeper principle: separate *thinking* from *formatting*, and ask for both, in that order. Most people collapse them and get slides that summarize. You want slides that argue. The only hard constraint is honesty — the model will happily generate plausible segment breakdowns, competitor context, and cohort charts you never gave it. Pin it to your real numbers and make it name its own gaps. That constraint is what makes the rest of the ambition safe.
